title: Concurrency and thread safety
problem: Two threads increment the same counter a million times each and the total comes out short, with no exception and no error, only a wrong number.
summary: A race needs shared state and a mutation; remove either or guard it. Prefer immutability, then atomics, then locks; run work on bounded pools fed by blocking queues; acquire multiple locks in one global order; rely on happens-before for visibility.
catTip: Two cats, one bowl, no lock: the bowl is a race condition. Two cats, two bowls, each wanting the other's: deadlock. I propose bowl ordering by cat seniority, mine first.

recall.q: Two threads call hits++ on a shared long field. Why is the final count wrong, and what are the fixes in order of preference?
recall.a: hits++ is a read, an add and a write, so both threads can read the same value and one increment is lost. Prefer immutability (nothing shared is mutated), then an AtomicLong whose incrementAndGet is a single compare-and-swap, then a lock (synchronized or ReentrantLock) when several fields must change together.

guide.breaks: Shared mutable state without coordination produces wrong counts, corrupted collections and flags that other threads never see, and the bugs appear only under load and vanish in the debugger.
guide.tradeoffs: Locks cost contention and risk deadlock, atomics cover only one variable, immutability costs copies, and bounded pools and queues force you to decide what happens when they are full.
guide.explainSimply: When two people edit the same sticky note at once, one edit gets lost. You can give each person their own note, use a note that updates in one stroke, or have one pen that only one person holds at a time. Trouble starts when two people each hold a pen the other needs.
guide.hint: Count the steps hidden inside the ++ and ask what another thread can do between them.

meow: Read bowl, add kibble, write bowl. Other cat did the same in between. Kibble lost. Meow-tomic operations, please.

quiz.prompt: Two threads each increment a plain long field 1,000 times with hits++. Which statement about the final value is guaranteed?
options: It is exactly 2,000, because long writes are atomic on 64-bit machines
It is exactly 1,000, because one thread always wins
It is at most 2,000 and often less, because increments interleave and overwrite each other
An exception is thrown when the second thread writes
quiz.explanation: Each increment is a read, an add and a write that can interleave with the other thread's, so increments are lost silently. Even where a single long write is atomic, the three-step read-modify-write is not, so the first option confuses atomic writes with atomic updates.

quiz.prompt: Thread A locks account 1 and then waits for account 2; thread B locks account 2 and then waits for account 1. Which change prevents the deadlock?
options: Always acquire the two account locks in a fixed global order, for example ascending account id
Retry the whole transfer in a loop until it succeeds
Store the balances in AtomicLong fields
quiz.explanation: Deadlock needs locks taken in opposite orders, and a global order removes the cycle. volatile and AtomicLong address visibility and single-variable atomicity, not two locks held at once, and a retry loop around a deadlocked call never gets the chance to run.

cards.q: What does volatile give you, and what does it not?
cards.a: Visibility and ordering: a write to a volatile field happens-before every later read of it, so other threads see the new value. Not atomicity: a check-then-act or an increment on a volatile field is still a race. Use an atomic or a lock for compound actions.

cards.q: Why is Executors.newCachedThreadPool() risky for a request-handling service, and what is the alternative?
cards.a: It creates a new thread whenever none is idle, so a traffic spike becomes unbounded thread growth and memory pressure. Use a ThreadPoolExecutor with a fixed size and a bounded queue, and pick a rejection policy (CallerRunsPolicy applies back-pressure) so that overload is explicit.

glossary.note: An atomic instruction that sets a value only if it still equals the expected old value; Java exposes it as compareAndSet.

sources.title: Java SE 21 API: java.util.concurrent.Executors
sources.supports: newFixedThreadPool uses a shared unbounded queue; newCachedThreadPool creates new threads as needed; newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor creates an unbounded number of virtual threads

sources.title: Java SE 21 API: java.util.concurrent.ThreadPoolExecutor
sources.supports: bounded queues prevent resource exhaustion; rejection policies; CallerRunsPolicy runs the task on the submitting thread and slows submission
